en.statement: The main thread of a Node.js process runs JavaScript callbacks on one event loop.
en.explanation: The Don't Block guide says Node.js runs JavaScript initialization and callbacks on one Event Loop, also called the main thread, beside a Worker Pool of k threads.

source.title: Don't Block the Event Loop: callback execution

en.statement: Node.js assigns non-blocking network I/O to libuv's threadpool.
en.explanation: Node.js uses the operating system's asynchronous network interfaces.

source.title: Don't Block the Event Loop: network I/O

en.statement: fs.readFile() with a callback uses libuv's threadpool for its file operations.
en.explanation: libuv workers perform the file operations used by asynchronous fs.readFile().

en.statement: dns.lookup() runs a synchronous getaddrinfo() call on libuv's threadpool.
en.explanation: The asynchronous API delegates the blocking system call to a worker.

en.statement: dns.resolve4() consults /etc/hosts when resolving a host name.
en.explanation: dns.resolve4() queries DNS servers and ignores /etc/hosts.

en.statement: crypto.pbkdf2() with a callback computes its result on the event loop thread.
en.explanation: The asynchronous crypto.pbkdf2() computation runs in libuv's threadpool.

en.statement: Asynchronous zlib compression uses libuv's threadpool to perform the compression work.
en.explanation: libuv workers execute zlib operations submitted by the asynchronous API.

en.statement: Assigning process.env.UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE in user code reliably resizes libuv's threadpool.
en.explanation: Setting UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE from inside the process is not guaranteed to work, because the threadpool is created before user code runs; set it in the environment when starting node.

en.statement: Node.js moves JSON.parse() of a large string to its Worker Pool.
en.explanation: JSON.parse() executes on the calling JavaScript thread.

source.title: Don't Block the Event Loop: JSON DOS

en.statement: Node.js confines the slowdown from a long crypto task in libuv's threadpool to other crypto calls.
en.explanation: Because libuv's threadpool has a fixed size, a slow task in it degrades the performance of other, seemingly unrelated APIs that also run in the pool.

en.statement: Node.js runs the timers phase before poll in each event loop iteration.
en.explanation: Iteration timers run after poll; an initial timer pass precedes the loop.

source.title: The Node.js Event Loop: phase overview

en.statement: The event loop runs one callback from a phase's queue, then moves on to the next phase.
en.explanation: Each phase has a FIFO queue; the event loop runs its callbacks until the queue is exhausted or a maximum number has run, then moves to the next phase.

source.title: The Node.js Event Loop: event loop explained

en.statement: The pending callbacks phase runs I/O callbacks deferred from the previous iteration.
en.explanation: Some system-operation callbacks wait until this phase.

source.title: The Node.js Event Loop: pending callbacks

en.statement: The poll phase calculates how long Node.js should wait for I/O.
en.explanation: Poll determines its waiting duration before processing available events.

en.statement: With setImmediate() callbacks queued, the event loop waits in the poll phase for new I/O.
en.explanation: With immediates queued, the event loop ends the poll phase rather than waiting for new I/O.

en.statement: The check phase runs each callback scheduled by setImmediate().
en.explanation: Node.js invokes immediate callbacks during check.

en.statement: Node.js emits an abruptly closed socket's 'close' event in the close callbacks phase.
en.explanation: Abrupt handle closure uses the close callbacks phase.

source.title: The Node.js Event Loop: close callbacks

en.statement: A setTimeout() callback runs exactly delay milliseconds after the setTimeout() call.
en.explanation: The timers docs say the callback will likely not run in precisely delay milliseconds; Node.js calls it as close as possible to that time and makes no guarantee about exact timing.

en.statement: timeout.unref() cancels the timeout's scheduled callback.
en.explanation: unref() only stops the timer from keeping the process alive; if other activity keeps the event loop running, the callback still runs.

en.statement: The Learn event loop guide says the names process.nextTick() and setImmediate() match when each callback fires.
en.explanation: The Learn event loop guide says process.nextTick() fires immediately on the same phase and setImmediate() on the following iteration, so in essence the names should be swapped.

source.title: The Node.js Event Loop: process.nextTick() vs setImmediate()

en.statement: process.nextTick() defers its callback until the current JavaScript operation finishes.
en.explanation: The current operation finishes before its queued next tick callbacks run.

en.statement: In ES module top-level code, queueMicrotask() callbacks precede process.nextTick() callbacks queued there.
en.explanation: ES module evaluation already runs inside the microtask queue.

en.statement: A setImmediate() callback queued inside another immediate runs in the same event loop iteration.
en.explanation: Node.js defers the nested immediate to the next iteration.

en.statement: The Node.js docs favor queueMicrotask() over process.nextTick() for most userland deferrals.
en.explanation: The API docs recommend queueMicrotask() for portable deferred execution.

en.statement: Recursive process.nextTick() calls give the poll phase a turn between queued callbacks.
en.explanation: The next tick queue can keep refilling and starve I/O.

en.statement: In the main CommonJS module, Node.js runs setTimeout(fn, 0) ahead of a setImmediate(fn) queued right after it.
en.explanation: Outside an I/O cycle, as in the main module, the order of setTimeout(fn, 0) and setImmediate(fn) callbacks is non-deterministic and depends on process performance.

source.title: The Node.js Event Loop: setImmediate() vs setTimeout()

en.statement: Inside an I/O callback, setImmediate(fn) runs before setTimeout(fn, 0) when both are scheduled there.
en.explanation: An immediate scheduled during I/O precedes the zero-delay timeout.

source.title: The Node.js Event Loop: immediate versus timeout

en.statement: setTimeout() from node:timers/promises fulfills its promise with the supplied value.
en.explanation: The optional value becomes the promise's fulfillment result.

en.statement: Aborting a pending node:timers/promises timeout via its supplied signal fulfills the promise early.
en.explanation: Cancelling with AbortSignal rejects the timer promise with AbortError.

en.statement: By default, Node.js loads a .mjs file as an ES module in a package with "type": "commonjs".
en.explanation: The .mjs extension determines the file's module format.

en.statement: Node.js takes a .js file's "type" from the project's root package.json despite a nearer package.json.
en.explanation: The nearest parent package.json supplies the controlling type field.

en.statement: An import() expression makes an ambiguous .js file qualify as an ES module during syntax detection.
en.explanation: Dynamic import() is valid in CommonJS, so it is not a detection marker.

en.statement: The packages docs recommend an explicit "type" field even for packages whose sources are CommonJS.
en.explanation: Explicit type metadata makes module interpretation predictable.

en.statement: Node.js resolves `import './utils'` to ./utils/index.js when utils is a directory.
en.explanation: A directory index import needs the complete path, including index.js.

en.statement: In a CommonJS module, Node.js requires the node: prefix to load the built-in test runner.
en.explanation: The built-in test runner is addressed as node:test.

source.title: CommonJS modules: built-in modules with mandatory node: prefix

en.statement: Node.js derives CommonJS named exports for ES module imports by evaluating the module's export object.
en.explanation: Node.js detects these names through heuristic static analysis.

en.statement: In a .cjs file, require() waits for an ES module dependency's top-level await before returning.
en.explanation: Top-level await anywhere in the graph triggers ERR_REQUIRE_ASYNC_MODULE.

source.title: CommonJS modules: loading ECMAScript modules using require()

en.statement: In a .cjs file, require() of a .mjs file with `export default 7` returns a namespace with .default equal to 7.
en.explanation: The default export occupies the namespace's default property.

source.title: CommonJS modules: loading ECMAScript modules using require()

en.statement: Node.js chooses "main" ahead of "exports" when a package defines both entry fields.
en.explanation: For package entry points, Node.js selects exports ahead of main.

en.statement: Node.js permits `pkg/package.json` imports when `pkg` omits that subpath from "exports".
en.explanation: Node.js rejects unlisted package-name subpaths, including package.json, with ERR_PACKAGE_PATH_NOT_EXPORTED.

en.statement: Node.js treats "exports": "./index.js" as a mapping for the package's "." entry.
en.explanation: A string "exports" value abbreviates a single "." entry.

en.statement: Node.js restricts "*" in a subpath export pattern to a single path segment.
en.explanation: The "*" replacement text can include "/" and nested paths.

en.statement: Node.js excludes a package subpath from an export pattern when its target is null.
en.explanation: Null exports targets exclude subpaths from broader patterns.

en.statement: Node.js ranks matching conditional exports by the specificity of their condition names.
en.explanation: Node.js checks keys in order; the first matching condition wins.

en.statement: The target file's ES module format activates the "import" export condition.
en.explanation: The "import" condition matches import requests, even when their target uses CommonJS.

en.statement: Node.js resumes parent condition matching when nested matching fails to select a mapping.
en.explanation: When nested export conditions produce no mapping, Node.js tries the remaining parent conditions.

en.statement: Node.js resolves package "imports" mappings through specifiers that start with "#".
en.explanation: The "#" prefix marks private package import specifiers.

en.statement: Node.js limits targets in a package's "imports" field to files inside that package.
en.explanation: An "imports" target may refer to an external package.

en.statement: The fs docs advise checking a file with fs.access() before calling fs.readFile() on it.
en.explanation: The fs docs advise against an fs.access() check before fs.open(), readFile() or writeFile(), because the file can change between the calls; open or read it directly and handle the error.

en.statement: fs.mkdir() with { recursive: true } reports an error when the target directory exists.
en.explanation: An existing directory by itself does not make recursive fs.mkdir() fail.

en.statement: On a local filesystem, `fs.open(path, 'wx', cb)` fails when the path already exists.
en.explanation: The 'wx' flag requests exclusive file creation, protecting an existing path from replacement.

en.statement: fs.cp() includes a directory's subdirectories in a copy with its default options.
en.explanation: fs.cp() defaults recursive to false; copying a directory tree needs recursive: true.

en.statement: `path.join('logs', 'today.txt')` prefixes its result with the current working directory.
en.explanation: path.join('logs', 'today.txt') produces the relative path 'logs/today.txt'.

en.statement: `path.resolve('/srv', '/tmp', 'app.js')` returns '/tmp/app.js'.
en.explanation: path.resolve() works from the right; the absolute '/tmp' makes it discard the earlier '/srv'.

en.statement: The fs APIs resolve relative string paths from the directory containing the ES module.
en.explanation: File system APIs resolve relative string paths against process.cwd().

en.statement: On macOS, path.basename() treats Windows backslashes as ordinary filename characters.
en.explanation: The default path API follows macOS rules; path.win32 handles Windows separators.

en.statement: EventEmitter removes a once() listener before it invokes that listener.
en.explanation: Removing a once() registration first prevents a recursive emit from reusing that registration.

en.statement: An EventEmitter's emit() call returns the value supplied by the last listener it invokes.
en.explanation: emit() returns whether listeners exist, ignoring their return values.

en.statement: EventEmitter invokes a regular function listener with `this` set to undefined.
en.explanation: A regular function listener receives the emitting EventEmitter as its this value.

en.statement: For an EventEmitter, `ee.prependListener("x", a); ee.prependListener("x", b)` puts b ahead of a.
en.explanation: Later prependListener() calls place listeners ahead of earlier prepends.

en.statement: EventEmitter turns an unhandled 'error' event into a process warning.
en.explanation: An unhandled 'error' event throws and ordinarily terminates the process.

en.statement: An events.errorMonitor listener consumes an EventEmitter's otherwise unhandled 'error' event.
en.explanation: events.errorMonitor observes errors; handling them needs an 'error' listener.

en.statement: EventEmitter refuses another listener when an event reaches the emitter's configured listener limit.
en.explanation: EventEmitter accepts extra listeners and emits MaxListenersExceededWarning when the threshold is exceeded.

en.statement: events.once(emitter, 'ready') rejects its promise if the emitter emits 'error' while waiting.
en.explanation: events.once(emitter, 'ready') rejects with the emitted error.

en.statement: events.on() returns an async iterator whose values contain arguments passed to the named event.
en.explanation: events.on() yields an array of arguments for each event.

en.statement: A Readable in object mode delivers `push(null)` to its consumer as a regular data item.
en.explanation: Readable reserves push(null) for signaling the end of data, including in object mode.

en.statement: `writable.write(chunk)` returning false means the stream discards that chunk.
en.explanation: writable.write() accepts the chunk despite returning false; wait for 'drain' before writing more.

en.statement: A fresh Readable enters flowing mode when you attach a 'data' listener.
en.explanation: A new Readable starts delivering chunks through events after a 'data' listener is attached.

en.statement: `stream.pipeline()` cleans up its streams when an error interrupts the transfer.
en.explanation: stream.pipeline() destroys its active streams when a transfer fails.

en.statement: Breaking out of `for await...of` over a Readable leaves the stream usable by default.
en.explanation: The default async iterator destroys the Readable when the loop exits through break.

en.statement: `buf instanceof Uint8Array` evaluates to true when buf is a Buffer.
en.explanation: Buffer extends Uint8Array, so its instances belong to both classes.

en.statement: Buffer.allocUnsafe() fills its result with zero bytes by default.
en.explanation: Buffer.allocUnsafe() leaves memory uninitialized; returned bytes may contain earlier data.

en.statement: Buffer.from('hello') uses UTF-8 to encode the string by default.
en.explanation: Buffer.from(string) selects utf8 when the encoding argument is omitted.

en.statement: Buffer.from(arrayBuffer) makes an independent copy of the ArrayBuffer's bytes.
en.explanation: Buffer.from(arrayBuffer) shares the ArrayBuffer's storage rather than copying its bytes.

en.statement: The UTF-8 byte count from `Buffer.byteLength('é', 'utf8')` is larger than `'é'.length`.
en.explanation: Buffer.byteLength() measures encoded bytes; UTF-8 uses two bytes for é.

en.statement: Node.js places the complete HTTP request body in an IncomingMessage object's body property.
en.explanation: IncomingMessage is a Readable stream; consume its body in chunks.

en.statement: A ServerResponse completes its response when application code calls its write() method.
en.explanation: response.end() completes the response; response.write() sends body chunks.

en.statement: response.writeHead() values override headers set earlier with response.setHeader().
en.explanation: When response.setHeader() and response.writeHead() supply the same header, the value passed to writeHead() wins.

en.statement: Node.js exposes an incoming HTTP request's header names in lowercase through req.headers.
en.explanation: IncomingMessage.headers normalizes the request's header names to lowercase.

en.statement: http.globalAgent uses HTTP Keep-Alive by default for requests that share its connection pool.
en.explanation: http.globalAgent retains connections for reuse by later requests.

en.statement: Node.js makes fetch() available as a global function to scripts started with the node executable.
en.explanation: Node.js scripts use global fetch() to issue HTTP requests.

en.statement: A Hash object accepts more input through update() after its digest() call returns.
en.explanation: hash.digest() finalizes the Hash; a later hash.update() call throws.

en.statement: crypto.timingSafeEqual() returns false when its input buffers have different byte lengths.
en.explanation: Inputs with different byte lengths cause crypto.timingSafeEqual() to throw.

en.statement: By default, globalThis.crypto exposes the functions exported by the node:crypto module.
en.explanation: globalThis.crypto implements the Web Crypto API, not node:crypto's API.

en.statement: child_process.spawn() launches its command through a shell by default.
en.explanation: child_process.spawn() uses shell: false by default. Set the shell option explicitly to run a command through a shell.

en.statement: child_process.exec() buffers the child's stdout and stderr for its completion callback.
en.explanation: The exec() callback receives the child's collected stdout and stderr after the child terminates.

en.statement: child_process.fork() opens an IPC channel to the Node.js process it starts.
en.explanation: fork() creates an IPC connection for the parent and child. They exchange messages through send() and the 'message' event.

en.statement: child_process.fork() can start its child through a shell when shell: true is set.
en.explanation: child_process.fork() ignores the shell option, including shell: true.

en.statement: An unread stdout pipe can block a child once the pipe's buffer fills.
en.explanation: Child-process pipes have limited capacity. If the parent leaves stdout unread, the child can wait for space before writing more.

en.statement: A child inherits parent variables omitted from its options.env object.
en.explanation: An options.env object supplies the child's environment rather than merging with process.env. Include the desired parent variables in that object.

en.statement: worker.postMessage() serializes message values according to the JSON data model.
en.explanation: worker.postMessage() uses the HTML structured clone algorithm. Its supported values include cyclic objects and Maps.

en.statement: A Worker can receive a SharedArrayBuffer in a message while its parent retains access.
en.explanation: A SharedArrayBuffer travels in the message value and stays accessible to both threads. It is excluded from transferList.

en.statement: A new Worker receives its own copy of process.env by default.
en.explanation: The Worker constructor copies its parent's environment. Changes to one thread's copy stay local unless the Worker uses SHARE_ENV.

en.statement: In a Worker, process.exit() terminates the parent Node.js process.
en.explanation: Inside a Worker, process.exit() stops the current thread rather than terminating the entire process.

en.statement: A Worker can receive SIGTERM through the process.on('SIGTERM') listener it registers.
en.explanation: Node.js does not deliver signals to Worker threads through process.on(). Signal event handling belongs to the process's main thread.

en.statement: fs.readFile() passes null in its callback's error slot after a successful read.
en.explanation: The first argument in fs.readFile()'s error-first callback is null on success, marking the read as successful.

en.statement: A try...catch around fs.readFile() catches an exception thrown later by its callback.
en.explanation: A try...catch around fs.readFile() has finished by the time its asynchronous callback runs. A throw inside that callback needs handling within that later execution.

en.statement: Node.js runs with `throw` as the default mode of the --unhandled-rejections command-line option.
en.explanation: throw is the default --unhandled-rejections mode. This mode begins by emitting 'unhandledRejection'.

en.statement: In throw mode, Node.js automatically escalates later unhandled rejections despite an 'unhandledRejection' listener.
en.explanation: In throw mode, an 'unhandledRejection' listener prevents automatic escalation of later unhandled rejections to uncaught exceptions.

en.statement: Node.js raises entry-point ES module static loading rejections as uncaught exceptions in `warn` mode.
en.explanation: A rejection during the entry point's ES module static loading phase becomes an uncaught exception regardless of the selected unhandled-rejection mode.

en.statement: The Node.js docs recommend resuming normal work after an 'uncaughtException' listener returns.
en.explanation: The process docs reserve 'uncaughtException' for last-resort synchronous cleanup before shutdown, because the application's state may be corrupted.

en.statement: With default handlers, Node.js automatically exits with code 1 after an uncaught exception.
en.explanation: Default uncaught-exception handling prints the stack to stderr and overrides any earlier process.exitCode.

en.statement: Node.js sends an exception thrown by an 'uncaughtException' listener back to that listener.
en.explanation: A throw inside an 'uncaughtException' listener terminates the process. Node.js skips recursive handling to avoid an infinite loop.

en.statement: For an escalated promise rejection, Node.js passes 'unhandledRejection' as the 'uncaughtException' origin.
en.explanation: When Node.js raises an unhandled promise rejection as an uncaught exception, the listener's origin argument is 'unhandledRejection'.

en.statement: Node.js invokes 'uncaughtExceptionMonitor' listeners before 'uncaughtException' listeners.
en.explanation: Node.js emits 'uncaughtExceptionMonitor' before its main exception handling. The monitor observes the failure while the existing handling policy stays in place.

en.statement: Node.js preserves an error's message text across patch releases within the same major line.
en.explanation: error.code is the stable identifier for Node.js errors. The message text may change in any release.

en.statement: An environment variable present in process.env has a string value.
en.explanation: Environment variables accessed through process.env have string values, even when their text represents numbers or booleans.

en.statement: --env-file overrides an environment variable that the launching process already provides.
en.explanation: A value already present in the process environment takes precedence over the same variable in an --env-file file.

en.statement: A variable defined in two --env-file files takes its value from the later file.
en.explanation: Node.js loads several --env-file files in command-line order, and a later file overrides values loaded from earlier ones.

en.statement: process.loadEnvFile() applies the NODE_OPTIONS settings found in the file it loads.
en.explanation: process.loadEnvFile() loads variables into process.env after startup. NODE_OPTIONS from that file has no effect on Node.js.

en.statement: For `node app.js`, process.argv starts with the absolute path to app.js.
en.explanation: For node app.js, process.argv[0] is the Node.js executable path. The script's absolute path is at process.argv[1].

en.statement: process.execArgv contains Node.js startup options that precede the script path.
en.explanation: process.execArgv records command-line options interpreted by Node.js before the program entry point. It excludes the script's own arguments.

en.statement: process.exit() waits for pending writes to process.stdout before ending the process.
en.explanation: process.exit() forces termination and can abandon pending stdout writes. Set process.exitCode to let the process finish its work before exiting.

en.statement: process.exit() makes Node.js emit 'beforeExit' before it emits 'exit'.
en.explanation: Node.js skips 'beforeExit' when process.exit() is called explicitly. That event concerns an event loop that runs out of work.

en.statement: Node.js abandons setTimeout() callbacks queued by an 'exit' listener when the process terminates.
en.explanation: Node.js terminates after 'exit' listeners return, abandoning their scheduled timer callbacks. Finish cleanup synchronously in the listener.

en.statement: On macOS, a SIGTERM listener replaces Node.js's default exit behavior for that signal.
en.explanation: Installing a SIGTERM listener removes Node.js's default handler on non-Windows platforms. The listener defines the response to that signal.

en.statement: process.on('SIGKILL', handler) registers handler for a SIGKILL signal.
en.explanation: Node.js rejects installing a SIGKILL listener. Its process signal API does not offer a handler for that signal.

en.statement: A node:test test passes when its completion callback succeeds and its returned promise fulfills.
en.explanation: node:test fails a test function that both receives a completion callback and returns a promise, even when both signal success.

en.statement: With `node --test`, it.only() makes Node.js skip the other tests in that file.
en.explanation: The only option takes effect when Node.js runs with --test-only or with test isolation disabled; plain `node --test` still runs every test in the file.

en.statement: By default, `node --test` runs each matching test file in its own child process.
en.explanation: The test runner isolates files in separate child processes. Tests defined within one file execute inside that file's process.

en.statement: On macOS, `node --watch-path=./src app.js` also restarts when an imported module outside ./src changes.
en.explanation: --watch-path restarts the process for changes in the given paths and turns off watching of required or imported modules, even when combined with --watch.

en.statement: Node.js executes `const port: number = '8080'` in a .ts file using built-in type stripping.
en.explanation: Node.js strips erasable TypeScript annotations without checking types, so the mismatched assignment still executes.

en.statement: Node.js reports a resolution error for an import that relies solely on a tsconfig.json paths mapping.
en.explanation: Node.js ignores tsconfig.json during native TypeScript execution, including its paths mappings. An import needs a specifier Node.js can resolve itself.

en.statement: Node.js converts enum declarations to JavaScript when it runs .ts files by default.
en.explanation: Built-in type stripping rejects enum declarations with ERR_UNSUPPORTED_TYPESCRIPT_SYNTAX because they require JavaScript generation.

en.statement: Node.js erases `import { Config } from './config.ts'` when Config is used solely as a type.
en.explanation: Node.js treats an import lacking the type keyword as a value import. Use import type for imports that need removal during type stripping.

en.statement: With --permission, --allow-fs-read=./data grants reads inside an existing data directory.
en.explanation: For an existing directory, the Permission Model expands its read grant to cover paths inside that directory.

en.statement: The Node.js docs present the Permission Model as protection against malicious code.
en.explanation: The Node.js docs describe the Permission Model as a seat belt for trusted code. Malicious code can bypass its restrictions.

en.statement: Up to Node.js 26, the Release working group targets Current for most nonbreaking main-branch changes.
en.explanation: The Release working group's policy brings most nonbreaking changes from main into Current releases.

en.statement: Up to Node.js 26, Active LTS automatically adopts the feature additions made in Current releases.
en.explanation: The Release team selects Active LTS features after checking their suitability and stability for the release line.

en.statement: The Releases page recommends Active LTS or Maintenance LTS releases for production applications.
en.explanation: The Releases page directs production users to these supported LTS phases.

en.statement: Up to Node.js 26, Node.js promotes a release line to LTS by publishing a new semver-major version.
en.explanation: LTS promotion happens in a semver-minor release of the existing major line.

en.statement: Up to Node.js 26, even-numbered release lines move from Current to Active LTS.
en.explanation: The historical schedule promotes even-numbered lines to Active LTS after their Current phase.

en.statement: Starting with Node.js 27, Node.js publishes a new major as Current in October.
en.explanation: The annual schedule starts the new Current major in April.

en.statement: Starting with Node.js 27, odd-numbered release lines finish support after their Current phase.
en.explanation: The annual model promotes odd-numbered major lines to LTS too.

en.statement: Starting with Node.js 27, Alpha releases can include semver-major API changes within the same release line.
en.explanation: The Alpha channel accepts breaking changes between prereleases for compatibility testing.

en.statement: Starting with Node.js 27, Alpha releases use the same testing policy as Node.js Nightly builds.
en.explanation: Alpha prereleases undergo project testing; the blog describes Nightly builds as automated and untested.

en.statement: Starting with Node.js 27, the support window spans 36 months from the first Current release.
en.explanation: Node.js starts this clock at Current; the preceding Alpha phase sits outside the support window.
